metadata.title: Shaping Students’ Financial Literacy: The Role of Parents and Socio-Economic Backgrounds

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus uses PISA 2022 financial literacy results aggregated at the country/economy level (e.g., percentages below Level 2 and mean score differences by ESCS quarter and parental interaction/autonomy items). The document does not report the specific student sampling weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures, but it relies on OECD’s published PISA 2022 database tables and associated statistical guidance. Because the analysis is presented as descriptive and equity-focused comparisons (e.g., score-point gaps and explained variation), the paper does not provide enough methodological detail to confirm whether complex survey weights (and which ones) were applied at the estimation stage. For analysts reproducing these results from microdata, PISA’s complex sampling design and plausible-value scaling should be handled using the official PISA weight and replicate-weight specifications provided with the PISA 2022 database.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable here because the document is a PISA in Focus policy brief that reports OECD-published proficiency levels (e.g., Level 2 thresholds) and mean score differences using already-processed PISA 2022 outputs, without describing an original student-level PV estimation procedure. Missing-data handling is not reported because the brief does not provide the underlying microdata processing or imputation/deletion rules; it instead cites OECD PISA 2022 database tables as the source of the reported estimates. This is therefore a reporting/availability limitation for methodological transparency rather than evidence that missing-data handling was unnecessary.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief uses PISA 2022 financial literacy assessment results for participating OECD countries and economies, reporting (i) the proportion of students below Level 2 proficiency and (ii) mean score differences and explained variation by ESCS quarter and parental interaction/autonomy questionnaire items. It does not specify any additional student-level inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., grade subsamples, item-completion thresholds, or missing-data exclusions) because it presents OECD-published database table outputs rather than a newly estimated microdata model.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus summarizes PISA 2022 financial literacy results for 15-year-old students, defining baseline financial literacy as reaching at least Level 2 in the financial literacy assessment. Across OECD countries and economies, nearly one in five students (18%) did not reach Level 2, rising to 26% when considering all participating countries and economies. The brief reports a large socio-economic gradient: advantaged students score 87 points higher than disadvantaged students on average (more than one proficiency level), and ESCS accounts for 12% of variation in financial literacy performance on average. It also highlights associations with parental interactions and autonomy: students who discuss spending-related topics with parents weekly or monthly perform better, and students who report independent spending autonomy score about 30 points higher after accounting for student characteristics. The document cautions that PISA data do not support causal claims, and it flags that some country estimates may be affected when PISA sampling standards are not met.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive policy brief based on OECD’s published PISA 2022 database tables rather than an original empirical ML study. As a result, it does not report an analytic sample size, PV estimation procedure, missing-data handling strategy, or any ML model training/evaluation outputs. The extraction therefore leaves ML-related fields empty and focuses on the reported proficiency benchmarks and equity comparisons.
